maths_eduqas_h.2.2.summary: Mastering scale factors, scale diagrams, and maps requires a seamless fluency in converting between ratio representations and real-world dimensions. Top-tier Grade 9 responses depend on recognising the multiplicative link between lengths, as well as handling area and volume scaling correctly when given linear multipliers. Precision with units, map scales, and bearings on scale drawings are essential core skills for both non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.p: A scale factor is a multiplier that describes how much a figure or dimension is enlarged or reduced. When dealing with linear scale factors, every corresponding length is multiplied by the exact same value.
bullets: A scale factor greater than 1 represents an enlargement.
A scale factor between 0 and 1 represents a reduction.
A scale factor of 1 means the shape remains congruent.
Corresponding lengths scale linearly, meaning if scale factor is k, length becomes k times original.

callouts.p: The ratio of any two corresponding lengths in two similar geometric figures.
Never apply a linear scale factor directly to areas or volumes without squaring or cubing it first.

core.p: Maps represent large geographical areas on a small sheet of paper by using a fixed ratio. To interpret a map scale correctly, both sides of the ratio must be in the exact same unit of measurement.
bullets: A map scale of 1:50000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50000 cm in real life.
Always convert centimetres to metres or kilometres to make real-life distances meaningful.
100 cm = 1 m, and 100000 cm = 1 km.
Map ratios are dimensionless, meaning units cancel out when written purely as a ratio.

callouts.p: Always convert map measurements into the same physical units before attempting any calculation.

fig.cap: Visual representation of map scale conversion from cm to km.

core.p: Scale diagrams require precise measurements using a ruler and protractor. Every line segment must be drawn to the exact specified proportion to earn full marks in examination conditions.
bullets: Read the given scale carefully, such as '1 cm represents 2 metres'.
Use a sharp pencil and a clean plastic ruler for accuracy.
Check that right angles are constructed accurately using set squares or protractors.
Label all vertices and key dimensions clearly on the final diagram.

callouts.p: Examiners generally allow a tolerance of +/- 2 mm for plotted lengths and +/- 2 degrees for angles.

core.p: Many maps and architectural plans use a visual scale bar instead of a written ratio. A scale bar remains accurate even if the map or diagram is photocopied or resized digitally.
bullets: Measure the physical length of the scale bar using your ruler.
Set up an equivalence equation between measured cm and real-world units.
Measure the distance required on the diagram and multiply by the scale factor derived from the bar.
Avoid relying on printed numbers if the page has been scaled; always measure the bar itself.

callouts.p: Scale bars resize proportionally with the image, making them immune to digital resizing errors.

core.p: When a two-dimensional shape is enlarged by a linear scale factor k, its area does not scale by k. Because area depends on two dimensions (length and width), the area scale factor is k squared.
bullets: If linear scale factor is k, then Area Scale Factor = k squared.
If a shape is enlarged by scale factor 3, its area increases by a factor of 3 squared = 9.
To find the real area, multiply the scale diagram area by k squared.
To find the real linear dimension from an area ratio, take the square root of the area scale factor.

callouts.p: Ratio of areas of similar figures = (Linear Scale Factor)^2.

core.p: Three-dimensional similar shapes scale in volume according to the cube of the linear scale factor. Length, width, and height all scale by k, meaning volume scales by k cubed.
bullets: If linear scale factor is k, then Volume Scale Factor = k cubed.
If a solid is enlarged by scale factor 2, its volume increases by 2 cubed = 8 times.
To find the real volume, multiply the model volume by k cubed.
To find the linear scale factor from volumes, calculate the cube root of the volume ratio.

callouts.p: A common Grade 8/9 error is multiplying volume by 3 instead of cubing the linear scale factor.

core.p: Navigation problems frequently combine scale diagrams with three-figure bearings. A bearing is measured clockwise from North and must always be written using exactly three digits.
bullets: Always draw a faint North line at every point where a bearing is measured.
Measure angles clockwise from the North line using a protractor.
Combine scale length conversion with accurate angle plotting to locate positions.
Use alternate interior angles (Z-angles) on parallel North lines for back-bearings.

callouts.p: Draw North lines lightly in pencil at every turning point to prevent angular misreadings.

fig.cap: Plotting a bearing of 065 degrees from point A on a scale drawing.

core.h: Converting Units of Area and Volume in Scaling
core.p: When dealing with scaled units, changing units before applying the scale factor is much safer than converting squared or cubed units afterwards.
bullets: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 square metre = 100 cm x 100 cm = 10,000 square cm.
1 m = 100 cm, so 1 cubic metre = 100 cm x 100 cm x 100 cm = 1,000,000 cubic cm.
Convert linear dimensions first, then calculate area or volume.
Always check whether the question asks for cm squared or m squared.

callouts.p: Square the conversion factor for area; cube the conversion factor for volume.

core.p: Professional blueprints use standard ratios such as 1:50 or 1:100. Interpreting these requires translating floor plans into actual room dimensions and calculating total materials required.
bullets: Measure the length of a room on the blueprint in centimetres.
Multiply by the scale factor denominator to find the real-life measurement in centimetres.
Convert centimetres into metres for practical building dimensions.
Calculate real floor areas using area scale factors or by converting dimensions before multiplying.

callouts.p: Convert the map scale into a direct multiplier (e.g. 1 cm = 0.5 m) to speed up calculations.

core.p: Exam questions frequently provide the real-life dimension and ask you to find the measurement on a map or scale model. This requires dividing by the scale factor rather than multiplying.
bullets: Identify the scale ratio in the form 1 : n.
To go from real life to map/model, divide the real measurement by n.
Ensure both quantities are in the exact same unit before dividing.
Check that your final answer on the map is smaller when reducing to scale.

callouts.p: Do not multiply real-life values by the scale factor when trying to find map lengths; always divide.

core.p: Higher tier papers combine scale factors with compound measures such as density, speed, and pressure, requiring multi-step logical deductions.
bullets: If a scale model is made of the same material as the real object, its volume scales by k cubed.
Mass = Density x Volume. Since density is constant, mass scales by the exact same factor as volume (k cubed).
Check whether surface area scaling or volume scaling is required for pressure calculations (Pressure = Force / Area).
Set up clear proportional equations for each compound component.

callouts.p: Mass is directly proportional to volume for uniform material, so mass scales by k cubed.

analogy.p: Imagine building an OO-gauge model railway layout where the scale is 1:76. Every single dimension of a real locomotive is divided by 76 so it fits on your table. However, if you want to know how much heavier the real train is, you cannot just multiply by 76; because the train has length, width, and height, the real train's volume and mass are 76 cubed times heavier than the model. The analogy breaks down because real materials cannot always be scaled down in thickness while maintaining structural integrity (the square-cube law in biology and engineering).

terms.d: The ratio by which any length of a geometric figure is enlarged or reduced.
Figures that have the same shape, equal corresponding angles, and sides in constant proportion.
The ratio of map distance to corresponding real-world ground distance.
A scale expressed as a ratio without units, such as 1:25000.
A graphic line divided into units representing real-world distances on a map.
The multiplier k applied to 1D lengths between similar figures.
The multiplier k squared applied to 2D areas between similar figures.
The multiplier k cubed applied to 3D volumes between similar figures.
A direction measured clockwise as a three-digit angle from North.
An architectural or engineering scale drawing used for construction.
Identical in shape and size.
A ratio where both quantities share identical units and cancel out.

mistakes.w: Multiplying area by the linear scale factor k instead of k squared.
mistakes.r: Area scale factor is always the square of the linear scale factor (k^2).

mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert units when calculating map distances (e.g. mixing cm and km directly).
mistakes.r: Always convert both quantities into the exact same unit before setting up equations.

mistakes.w: Multiplying volume by 3 instead of cubing the linear scale factor.
mistakes.r: Volume scale factor is the cube of the linear scale factor (k^3).

mistakes.w: Multiplying instead of dividing when working backwards from real life to a map length.
mistakes.r: Divide real-life dimensions by the scale factor denominator to find the map length.

mistakes.w: Writing a bearing with fewer than three digits, such as 65 degrees instead of 065 degrees.
mistakes.r: All bearings must be written as a three-digit number.
Bearings are strictly measured in a clockwise direction from the North line.

mistakes.w: Assuming density changes when scaling a solid object.
mistakes.r: Density remains constant for uniform materials; mass scales proportionally with volume.

exam.q: On a map with a scale of 1:25000, the distance between two towns is 6 cm. Calculate the real-life distance in kilometres.
exam.tip: Always remember there are 100,000 cm in 1 km.

exam.q: Two solid metal spheres are mathematically similar. The smaller sphere has a radius of 3 cm and the larger sphere has a radius of 9 cm. Find the volume scale factor.
exam.tip: Find the linear scale factor first, then cube it for volume.

exam.q: A model of a bridge is built to a scale of 1:200. The surface area of the model is 450 cm^2. Calculate the surface area of the real bridge in square metres.
model: Convert to m^2 by dividing by 10000
exam.tip: Convert cm^2 to m^2 by dividing by 10,000 at the end.

exam.q: A map has a scale bar where 2 cm represents 5 km. Express this scale in the form 1 : n.
exam.tip: Both sides of the ratio must represent the exact same unit (cm).

exam.q: The volume of a child's toy car is 120 cm^3. The real car has a volume of 15 m^3. Find the linear scale factor of the model.
model: Convert real volume to cm^3: 15 m^3 = 15,000,000 cm^3
Linear scale factor = cube root of 125,000
exam.tip: Ensure both volumes are in the same units before finding the ratio.

exam.q: Ship A sails on a bearing of 070 degrees from port P for 8 cm on a scale drawing where 1 cm represents 10 km. Find the distance from port P in km.
model: Bearing 070 degrees is used for direction, distance is purely 80 km

exam.q: Two similar containers have heights of 12 cm and 18 cm. The smaller container holds 400 ml of water. Work out the capacity of the larger container.
exam.tip: Fractional linear scale factors cube cleanly using decimals or improper fractions.

exam.q: A rectangular park has an area of 0.12 km^2. On a plan, the area of the park is 30 cm^2. Find the map scale in the form 1 : n.
model: Linear scale factor = square root of 40,000,000
exam.tip: Be extremely careful with area unit conversions when squaring and rooting.

exam.q: A statue has a mass of 4.5 tonnes. A scale model of the statue is made from the same bronze material with a linear scale factor of 1:10. Find the mass of the model in kilograms.
model: Mass scales by the same factor as volume
exam.tip: Mass is proportional to volume when material density is uniform.

worked.q: A garden is represented on a plan with a scale of 1:200. On the plan, the rectangular lawn measures 6 cm by 4.5 cm. (a) Calculate the actual dimensions of the lawn in metres. (b) Calculate the actual area of the lawn in square metres.
steps: For part (a), multiply each plan dimension by 200 to get actual cm: Length = 6 x 200 = 1200 cm; Width = 4.5 x 200 = 900 cm.
Convert actual cm to metres by dividing by 100: Actual length = 12 m; Actual width = 9 m.
For part (b), calculate actual area directly: Area = 12 m x 9 m = 108 m^2.
Alternatively, use area scale factor: Plan area = 6 x 4.5 = 27 cm^2. Area scale factor = 200^2 = 40,000. Real area = 27 x 40,000 = 1,080,000 cm^2. Convert to m^2 by dividing by 10,000 to get 108 m^2.

worked.q: Two similar jugs, A and B, have base diameters of 8 cm and 12 cm respectively. Jug A has a height of 15 cm and holds 500 ml of juice. (a) Find the height of Jug B. (b) Find the capacity of Jug B in millilitres.
steps: Find the linear scale factor k from the given diameters: k = 12 / 8 = 1.5.
For part (a), multiply Jug A's height by the linear scale factor: Height of Jug B = 15 x 1.5 = 22.5 cm.
For part (b), calculate the volume scale factor by cubing the linear scale factor: Volume SF = 1.5 cubed = 3.375.
Multiply Jug A's capacity by the volume scale factor: Capacity of Jug B = 500 x 3.375 = 1687.5 ml.

maths_eduqas_h.2.8.summary: Mastering the connections between ratios, fractions, and linear functions is a crucial Grade 9 skill for the Eduqas GCSE Higher tier. This topic bridges the gap between arithmetic sharing and coordinate geometry, allowing you to represent ratios as coordinate pairs, algebraic lines, and proportional fractions. By understanding how parts of a ratio translate into fractional components of a whole and how those fractions form straight-line graphs, you unlock advanced problem-solving techniques for complex algebraic and geometric contexts.

core.p: Converting between ratios and fractions is the fundamental building block for higher-level proportional reasoning. When a quantity is split into a ratio a : b, the total number of parts is a + b. Each part can then be expressed as a fraction of the whole. This allows you to transition smoothly from comparing parts of a set to evaluating a part relative to the entire system.
bullets: For a ratio $a : b$, the total number of parts is $a + b$.
The first quantity represents the fraction $\frac{a}{a+b}$ of the total.
The second quantity represents the fraction $\frac{b}{a+b}$ of the total.
Fractions can be converted back to ratios by looking at the numerators of parts that share the same denominator.

callouts.p: If quantity $x$ and quantity $y$ are in the ratio $a : b$, then $x = \frac{a}{a+b} \times \text{Total}$ and $y = \frac{b}{a+b} \times \text{Total}.
Always sum the ratio parts first. Forgetting to add them together is the single most common error when converting ratios to fractions.

fig.cap: Visualising a 3:2 ratio divided into 5 total parts represented as fractions.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="40" width="360" height="60" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" rx="8"/><rect x="20" y="40" width="216" height="60" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" rx="0"/><line x1="236" y1="40" x2="236" y2="100" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="128" y="75" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Part A: 3/5</text><text x="308" y="75" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Part B: 2/5</text><text x="200" y="150" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1b2540">Total parts = 3 + 2 = 5</text></svg>

core.p: Going in reverse requires expressing given fractional amounts as a ratio in its simplest form. If you know that quantity P is $\frac{3}{7}$ of a total and quantity Q is $\frac{4}{7}$, the ratio P : Q is simply $3 : 4$. When fractions have different denominators, you must find a common denominator to compare them directly as a ratio.
bullets: If $A = \frac{2}{5}T$ and $B = \frac{3}{5}T$, then $A : B = 2 : 3$.
To compare fractional parts of different wholes, convert them to equivalent fractions with a common denominator.
Simplify integer ratios by dividing by the highest common factor (HCF).
Fractional ratios like $\frac{1}{2} : \frac{1}{3}$ are simplified by multiplying by the lowest common multiple (LCM) of denominators.

callouts.p: You cannot write a direct ratio of two quantities if they are fractions of different totals, unless you first scale them to the same absolute value.

core.p: Ratios can be treated as operators or multipliers that scale one quantity to find another. If $x : y = 4 : 7$, then $y = \frac{7}{4}x$ and $x = \frac{4}{7}y$. Viewing ratios as multiplicative operators connects directly to linear scaling and function notation.
bullets: The ratio $x : y = a : b$ can be written as the equation $y = \frac{b}{a}x$.
The multiplier $\frac{b}{a}$ acts as the scale factor transforming $x$ into $y$.
Inverse relationships are found by inverting the ratio fraction: if $y = \frac{b}{a}x$, then $x = \frac{a}{b}y$.
Multipliers can be decimals, fractions, or surds in higher-tier questions.

callouts.p: The multiplier $\frac{b}{a}$ is the constant of proportionality, often denoted as $k$, giving the direct proportion equation $y = kx.

core.p: A linear function is of the form $y = mx + c$. When two variables are in a constant ratio $x : y = a : b$, they form a direct proportion linear function passing through the origin, where the y-intercept $c = 0$ and the gradient $m = \frac{b}{a}$ (or $\frac{a}{b}$ depending on which variable is dependent).
bullets: The statement 'y is in a constant ratio to x' means $y = kx$ where $k$ is a constant.
The graph of a ratio relationship is a straight line through the origin $(0,0)$.
The gradient of the line represents the ratio value expressed as a unit rate.
Shifting the ratio relationship by a constant amount creates a linear function of the form $y = mx + c$ where $c \neq 0$.

callouts.p: A function representing a direct ratio has the form $f(x) = mx$ where $m > 0$.

fig.cap: Graph of a linear function representing the ratio y : x = 3 : 2 (i.e. y = 1.5x).
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="350" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="220" x2="80" y2="30" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="200" x2="320" y2="50" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><text x="340" y="215" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">x</text><text x="70" y="25" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">y</text><text x="190" y="115" font-size="12" fill="#2563eb">y = (3/2)x</text><circle cx="80" cy="200" r="4" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="200" cy="125" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/><circle cx="320" cy="50" r="4" fill="#2563eb"/></svg>

core.p: Any point $(x, y)$ lying on a line representing a ratio $a : b$ satisfies the condition that $x : y$ simplifies to $a : b$. In exam questions, you may be given coordinates and asked whether they satisfy a given ratio, or to find missing coordinates using proportional triangles under the line.
bullets: If point $(X, Y)$ lies on $y = \frac{b}{a}x$, then $X : Y = a : b$.
Similar right-angled triangles formed under the line confirm the constancy of the ratio.
Scaling coordinates by a factor $k$ moves along the line while preserving the ratio.
Algebraic coordinates like $(t, kt)$ always maintain the ratio $1 : k$.

callouts.p: Draw a right-angled triangle under the line with horizontal step $a$ and vertical rise $b$ to instantly read off the ratio.

core.p: Higher-tier Eduqas papers often link ratio statements directly to linear simultaneous equations. Translating a sentence like "the ratio of $x$ to $y$ is $2:3$, and their sum is $40$" into algebraic equations allows you to solve for both variables efficiently.
bullets: Translate ratio statements into algebraic equations: $x : y = a : b$ becomes $\frac{x}{y} = \frac{a}{b}$ or $bx = ay$.
Combine with linear constraint equations (e.g., $x + y = k$) to form a solvable system.
Use substitution: express one variable in terms of the other using the ratio multiplier, then substitute into the constraint equation.
Verify solutions by checking that the resulting values simplify back to the original ratio.

callouts.p: The ratio equation $\frac{x}{y} = \frac{a}{b}$ can be rewritten without fractions using cross-multiplication: $bx = ay$.

core.p: Connecting ratios to linear functions enables the coordinate geometry technique of dividing a line segment in a given ratio $m : n$. By examining the horizontal and vertical distances between two points, you can calculate the exact coordinates of the dividing point using linear fractional increments.
bullets: To divide line segment AB from $(x_1, y_1)$ to $(x_2, y_2)$ in the ratio $m : n$:
The x-coordinate is $x_1 + \frac{m}{m+n}(x_2 - x_1)$.
The y-coordinate is $y_1 + \frac{m}{m+n}(y_2 - y_1)$.
This is a direct application of fractional linear interpolation between two points.

callouts.p: Point dividing $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ in ratio $m:n$ is $\left( \frac{nx_1 + mx_2}{m+n}, \frac{ny_1 + my_2}{m+n} \right)$.

core.h: Direct Proportion and Linear Graphs ($y = kx$)
core.p: Direct proportion is a specific type of linear function where the graph is a straight line passing through the origin. The ratio between the two variables remains constant everywhere on the line. Understanding how to extract the ratio from the gradient is essential for top grades.
bullets: Equation format: $y = kx$, where $k$ is the constant of proportionality.
The ratio $y : x$ is always equal to $k : 1$.
The gradient of the line is equal to $k$.
Any point $(x, y)$ on the graph gives the ratio $x : y = 1 : k$ or $y : x = k : 1$.

callouts.p: If a straight line does not pass through $(0,5)$, the variables are NOT in direct proportion, even though the relationship is linear ($y = mx + c$). Ratios require $c = 0$.

core.h: Inverse Proportion and Hyperbolic Functions ($xy = k$)
core.p: While direct proportion relates to linear functions, inverse proportion relates to non-linear hyperbolic functions. If two variables are inversely proportional, their product is constant ($xy = k$). This means that as one variable increases, the other decreases in a non-linear fashion.
bullets: Equation format: $y = \frac{k}{x}$ or $xy = k$.
Can be viewed through reciprocal ratios: as $x$ scales by factor $n$, $y$ scales by factor $\frac{1}{n}$.
The graph is a rectangular hyperbola in the first and third quadrants.
Inverse proportion is tested on Higher tier papers to contrast with direct linear ratio functions.

callouts.p: In inverse proportion, the product of corresponding values is always constant: $x_1 y_1 = x_2 y_2 = k$.

core.p: Sometimes, exam questions require you to rearrange formulae where variables are defined by a ratio. For example, if the base and height of a triangle are in the ratio $3 : 4$, you can substitute $b = 3t$ and $h = 4t$ into the area formula to find an expression in terms of a single variable $t$.
bullets: Substitute ratio variables using a common scaling variable $t$.
For ratio $p : q : r$, let the quantities be $pt$, $qt$, and $rt$.
Substitute these expressions into geometric or algebraic formulae (Area, Volume, Perimeter).
Solve for $t$ and then back-substitute to find the individual actual lengths or quantities.

callouts.p: Introducing a dummy variable $t$ is the most robust way to handle multi-part ratio algebraic substitutions without making fraction errors.

core.p: Grade 9 questions often combine ratio, fractions, and linear functions in context. You might be given a cost function or a profit margin split in a ratio that changes dynamically with production volume $x$. Mastery requires setting up algebraic expressions for each part and equating them to given linear constraints.
bullets: Break down complex word problems into distinct linear expressions for each ratio part.
Form an equation representing the total sum or difference.
Solve for the scaling factor or variable.
Interpret your algebraic solution back into ratio and fractional terms as required by the final question prompt.

callouts.p: If the question asks for a fraction, do not leave your answer as a ratio. Always convert your final algebraic result into the exact format requested.

core.p: Higher tier Eduqas papers may express ratios using function notation. For instance, given a function $f(x)$, you may be told that $f(x) : x = 3 : 2$. This requires setting up the algebraic equation $\frac{f(x)}{x} = \frac{3}{2}$ and solving for the function itself, linking core algebra with ratio principles.
bullets: Translate $f(x) : g(x) = a : b$ into the algebraic fraction $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{a}{b}$.
Use cross-multiplication to find the functional relationship.
Evaluate the function at specific values of $x$ to find numerical ratio outputs.
Combine with composite and inverse functions in extension problems.

callouts.p: $f(x) : x = a : b \iff b f(x) = a x$ for all valid $x$.

analogy.p: Imagine making cordial squash: a recipe calls for juice and water in the ratio 1 : 4. This means juice is 1/5 of the total drink, and water is 4/5. If you plot the amount of juice ($x$) against water ($y$), you get a straight line $y = 4x$ passing through the origin with a gradient of 4. Where this analogy breaks down is that cordial mixing has physical capacity limits, whereas mathematical linear functions extend infinitely in both directions.

terms.d: A quantitative relation between two or more amounts showing the relative sizes of values.
A numerical quantity that is not a whole number, representing a part of a whole divided into equal parts.
A function whose graph is a straight line, typically written in the form $y = mx + c$.
A relationship between two quantities where the ratio of their values is constant ($y = kx$).
A relationship where an increase in one quantity results in a proportional decrease in the other ($xy = k$).
The constant multiplier $k$ that relates proportional quantities ($y = kx$).
A measure of the steepness of a line, calculated as vertical change divided by horizontal change.
The point where a graph crosses the y-axis, representing the value of $y$ when $x = 0$.
A fraction used to scale a quantity up or down in proportional calculations.
A technique to solve equation fractions by multiplying the numerator of one side by the denominator of the other.
Splitting a line segment into a given ratio using coordinate geometry fractions.
A method of writing algebraic rules using $f(x)$ to represent the output for input $x$.
A symbol, usually a letter, representing an unknown number in an expression or equation.
The state of being corresponding in size, degree, or intensity to something else.

mistakes.w: Writing the ratio $3 : 5$ as the fraction $\frac{3}{5}$ when referring to a part-to-part comparison
mistakes.r: Part-to-part ratios must use the sum of parts as the denominator for fractions of the whole: $\frac{3}{8}$ and $\frac{5}{8}$.

mistakes.w: Stating that $y = 2x + 3$ shows direct proportion because it involves multiplication
mistakes.r: Direct proportion requires a straight line passing through the origin ($c = 0$). Here, the y-intercept is 3.

mistakes.w: Inverting the fraction when converting a ratio $a : b$ into a linear function $y = mx$
mistakes.r: For ratio $x : y = a : b$, the function is $y = \frac{b}{a}x$, not $\frac{a}{b}x$.

mistakes.w: Dividing a quantity by the difference of ratio parts instead of their sum
mistakes.r: Always add the ratio parts together to find the total number of fractional parts ($a + b$).

mistakes.w: Assuming inverse proportion means negative gradient on a straight line
mistakes.r: Inverse proportion is represented by a curved rectangular hyperbola ($xy = k$), not a straight line.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include the scaling variable $t$ when substituting a ratio into an algebraic formula
mistakes.r: Use $3t$ and $4t$ instead of just $3$ and $4$ when side lengths are unknown.

mistakes.w: Mixing up dependent and independent variables on coordinate ratio graphs
mistakes.r: The first term in a ratio $x : y$ corresponds to the horizontal axis ($x$), and the second to the vertical axis ($y$).

exam.q: The ratio of red beads to blue beads in a bag is $3 : 5$. What fraction of the total beads are blue?
exam.tip: Always calculate the total number of parts by adding the ratio numbers together first.

exam.q: Express the linear function $y = \frac{3}{4}x$ as a ratio of $x : y$ in its simplest integer form.
exam.tip: Pay careful attention to whether the question asks for x : y or y : x.

exam.q: A line represents the ratio $x : y = 2 : 7$. Write down the equation of the linear function representing $y$ in terms of $x$.
exam.tip: The vertical variable $y$ is the numerator when finding $y$ in terms of $x$.

exam.q: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is $4 : 3$. There are 84 members in total. Use fractions to find the number of girls.
exam.tip: Convert the ratio to a fraction of the total before multiplying by the overall quantity.

exam.q: Point P divides the line segment from $(-2, 1)$ to $(8, 11)$ in the ratio $2 : 3$. Find the coordinates of P.
exam.tip: Use the fractional increment formula for internal division of coordinates.

exam.q: Two variables, $p$ and $q$, are in the ratio $p : q = 5 : 2$. If $p + q = 49$, find the value of $p$ using fractional multipliers.
exam.tip: Fractional multipliers streamline the calculation compared to finding the value of a single share.

exam.q: A straight-line graph passes through the origin and the point $(4, 10)$. Write the equation of the line representing this proportional ratio.
exam.tip: Since it passes through the origin, use y = kx where k is the y-coordinate divided by the x-coordinate.

exam.q: The ratio of two numbers is $3 : 7$. When 12 is added to each, the ratio becomes $5 : 9$. Find the original numbers.
exam.tip: Use algebraic multipliers ($3x$ and $7x$) and set up a fractional equation.

exam.q: State whether the linear function $3x - 4y = 0$ represents a direct ratio between $x$ and $y$. Give a reason.
model: It can be rearranged to y = (3/4)x, which passes through the origin with no constant term
exam.tip: Check if the equation simplifies to y = kx with zero intercept.

exam.q: The function $f(x)$ is such that $f(x) : x = 7 : 3$. Find $f(6)$.
exam.tip: Convert the functional ratio into an algebraic equation before substituting the value.

worked.q: The ratio of water to flour in a dough mixture is $3 : 5$ by weight. If the total weight of the dough is 1.6 kg, use fractions to find the weight of the flour in grams.
steps: Step 1: Find the total number of parts in the ratio. Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8 parts.
Step 2: Express the weight of flour as a fraction of the total dough. Flour fraction = 5/8.
Step 3: Calculate the weight of flour in kg by multiplying the fraction by the total weight. Flour weight = (5/8) x 1.6 kg = 1.0 kg.
Step 4: Convert the result into grams as requested by the question. 1.0 kg = 1000 grams.

worked.q: A straight line graph represents the ratio $y : x = 4 : 3$. (a) Write the equation of the line in the form $y = mx$. (b) Determine whether the point $(9, 11)$ lies on this line.
steps: Step 1: Translate the ratio $y : x = 4 : 3$ into a linear function. Since $y$ is the vertical axis and $x$ is the horizontal axis, $\frac{y}{x} = \frac{4}{3}$, giving $y = \frac{4}{3}x$.
Step 2: Test point $(9, 11)$ by substituting $x = 9$ into the equation. $y = \frac{4}{3}(9) = 12$.
Step 3: Compare the calculated $y$-value ($12$) with the given $y$-coordinate ($11$). Since $12 \neq 11$, the point does not lie on the line.
worked.ans: (a) y = (4/3)x (b) No, because when x = 9, y = 12, not 11.
